project_scope.note: Built from exact Schoenocaulon texanum video frames showing whole-plant habit, basal foliage, the flowering spike and individual flowers/anthers. The species remains taxonomy/range-pending and is not a canonical target-zone anchor yet.
project_scope.reference_status: taxonomy/range review required before canonical install

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with monocot habit and inflorescence architecture: many members are perennial herbs with basal or cauline leaves and a terminal spike or raceme of small three-merous flowers.
family_diagnostics.flower: Flowers commonly have 6 tepals and 6 stamens, although family diversity makes that pattern supportive rather than diagnostic by itself.
family_diagnostics.ovary: Superior in the typical family pattern.
family_diagnostics.underground: Perennial organs may include rhizomes, bulbs or corm-like structures depending on the lineage.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Six tepals is a weak character shared across many monocot families. Pair the flower with inflorescence architecture, ovary position, fruit and genus-level characters.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → inflorescence architecture → one flower → ovary/fruit confirmation
visual_lesson.intro: Melanthiaceae is a good reminder that some families are learned as a combination of characters rather than one magic field mark.

steps.title: 1 · Read the whole architecture
steps.photo_role: Schoenocaulon texanum whole-plant habit / basal leaves / flowering spike
steps.look_for: Basal foliage feeding into a conspicuous upright flowering spike.
steps.why_it_matters: The growth form is more useful than trying to identify a tiny six-part flower in isolation.

steps.title: 2 · Zoom into the spike
steps.look_for: Numerous small flowers arranged along the elongated inflorescence.
steps.why_it_matters: This connects whole-plant architecture to the individual floral units.

steps.title: 3 · Count the floral parts
steps.look_for: A three-merous monocot pattern, commonly expressed as 6 tepals and 6 stamens.
steps.why_it_matters: It confirms the monocot floral framework but should not be used alone to name the family.

steps.title: 4 · Confirm the reproductive end
steps.look_for: Locate the ovary above the attachment point of the other floral parts and, later, a capsule.
steps.why_it_matters: Ovary and fruit architecture provide the stronger tie-breakers once the six-tepal pattern has narrowed the field.

comparisons.title: Melanthiaceae vs Asparagaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can have six-tepaled monocot flowers, so do not separate them by tepal count alone. Use inflorescence, ovary/fruit characters and genus-level morphology.

comparisons.title: Why older books can be confusing
comparisons.rule: Several lineages now treated in Melanthiaceae were historically placed broadly in Liliaceae or allied families, so older names and family placements may differ.

visual_lesson.caveat: This is intentionally a combination-character lesson. Schoenocaulon texanum supplies strong video architecture, but the family should not be reduced to a single Schoenocaulon gestalt.
